title: Effect of sodium iodide addition on ion transport and electrochemical behavior of a free base electrolyte for magnesium–sulfur batteries
content: Rechargeable magnesium–sulfur (Mg–S) batteries are of interest for energy-storage applications but remain limited by slow Mg2+ transport, interfacial reactions, and polysulfide migration. In this work, sodium iodide (NaI) was introduced into a halogen-free Mg(NO3)2-based electrolyte containing acetonitrile and tetraethylene glycol dimethyl ether (HFE), and its influence on electrolyte properties and Mg–S cell behavior was investigated using a MoS2@SiC@C@S composite cathode. NaI addition increased the ionic conductivity at 303 K from 1.21 × 10−4 to 1.38 × 10−3 S cm−1 and the Mg2+ transference number from 0.438 to 0.704, while the apparent activation energy for ionic conduction decreased from 0.233 to 0.168 eV. These changes indicate improved ionic transport in the NaI-containing electrolyte. Electrochemical measurements showed differences in the Mg/electrolyte interfacial response and lower polarization during the initial Mg stripping/plating cycles, although the polarization increased during prolonged cycling. The oxidative decomposition onset also shifted from approximately 4.20 V for HFE to 3.86 V for HFE–NaI. Mg–S cells containing HFE–NaI delivered initial discharge/charge capacities of 1689.35/1209.99 mAh g−1 compared with 1303.91/821.48 mAh g−1 for HFE. A pencil-drawn graphite (PDG) layer was additionally examined as a simple modification of the Mg surface and resulted in lower polarization and more defined voltage profiles, although capacity fading remained evident. Overall, NaI addition modifies the transport and electrochemical characteristics of the halogen-free electrolyte and improves the initial Mg–S cell response, while further optimization is required to improve cycling stability.
